chapters.title: Chapter 3: India's Market Cycles, Era by Era

lessons.title: The Long Grind: Indian Markets from 2009 to 2014

body.text: A market can bounce back from a crash and still go nowhere for years. From January 2008 to the end of 2013 the Sensex made almost no net progress, inflation quietly took away a large share of investors' purchasing power, and a few sectors soared while others collapsed.

children.text: Crashes get the documentaries. Sideways markets get ignored, even though they are often harder on investors. This lesson covers the five years after the 2008 crash, when India's headline index recovered quickly and then stalled. It is the Indian version of the lesson from Japan in Lesson 2.4, on a much smaller scale: when the engines underneath a market are damaged, a rebound in prices is not the same as a new up cycle.
A Sharp Rebound, Then a Wall

India's response to the 2008 crisis was fast and large. The RBI cut its repo rate from 9% to 4.75% by April 2009, and the government cut excise duties and raised spending. Then politics added fuel. On 18 May 2009, the first trading day after a decisive general election result, the Sensex rose about 17% in a single session and hit its upper circuit limit, halting trading for the day. By November 2010 the index was back above 21,000, close to its 2008 peak. It looked like the next supercycle had begun. It had not.

markDefs.definition: A situation in which a country runs both a large government fiscal deficit and a large current account deficit, meaning it spends more than it earns both at home and with the rest of the world, and depends on foreign capital to fund the gap.
A widely used description of India's government in roughly 2011 to 2013, when major decisions on projects, land, mining and reforms were delayed amid corruption investigations and coalition politics.

children.text: The stimulus had revived demand, but it had also stoked inflation, and the investment boom of 2003 to 2008 had left behind heavily borrowed companies and half-built projects. Meanwhile corruption scandals froze government decision-making, a period widely described as
. Almost every engine from Chapter 1 was pointing the wrong way.

cells: Inflation and rates
Consumer inflation ran around 10% for much of 2012 and 2013. The RBI raised the repo rate 13 times between March 2010 and October 2011, from 4.75% to 8.5%
Rates pulling down P/E multiples, Lesson 1.3
Investment
Power, road, mining and steel projects stalled over land, environmental clearances and fuel supply. New private investment dried up
The Juglar investment cycle turning down, Lesson 1.2
Governance shocks

The 2G spectrum and coal block allocation controversies led the Supreme Court to cancel 122 telecom licences in 2012 and over 200 coal blocks in 2014. A retrospective tax amendment in 2012 alarmed foreign investors
Policy uncertainty raising the risk premium investors demand
Banks

Instead of recognising bad loans, banks restructured many of them, rolling over loans to struggling infrastructure, steel and airline companies. Kingfisher Airlines was grounded in 2012 owing banks thousands of crores
Zombie lending, a smaller version of Japan in Lesson 2.4
External balance
The current account deficit hit a record of about 4.8% of GDP in 2012-13, driven by oil and gold imports. India depended on foreign money to fund it
Vulnerability to a turn in the global credit cycle
Growth
GDP growth fell from above 9% before 2008 to below 5% in 2012-13 and 2013-14, as measured at the time
Earnings growth slowing, dragging on the trend line from Lesson 1.1

body.title: Sensex at major turning points, 2008 to 2014 (approximate)

children.text: The shape tells the story. After the rebound, the Sensex spent three years bouncing between roughly 15,000 and 21,000, each rally stalling near the old 2008 high. It only broke decisively higher in the run-up to the 2014 general election. An investor who bought at the January 2008 peak was roughly back to break-even by December 2013, six years later, in nominal terms.

body.label: Break-even is not the same as recovery
body.context: If the Sensex is at the same level after six years, and consumer prices rose about 9% a year, which is close to what Indian households experienced, the holding buys 1 ÷ 1.09 to the power 6, about 60% of what it did. Dividends offset only a small part of that.

events.title: A hint from Washington
events.description: US Federal Reserve chairman Ben Bernanke says the Fed could slow, or taper, its bond purchases. Global investors start pulling money out of emerging markets that depend on foreign capital.

events.title: Money leaves
events.description: Foreign investors sell Indian bonds and shares. The rupee slides from about 55 per dollar in May, and in August Morgan Stanley groups India with Brazil, Indonesia, South Africa and Turkey as the Fragile Five.

events.title: Emergency measures
events.description: The RBI tightens liquidity to defend the rupee, and the government raises the import duty on gold to 10% and restricts gold imports to cut the current account deficit.

events.title: The low point
events.description: The rupee touches about 68.85 per dollar, a record low at the time and about 20% weaker than in May. The Sensex falls to around 17,400.

events.title: Rajan arrives
events.description: Raghuram Rajan takes over as RBI Governor. A special swap window encourages banks to raise foreign currency deposits from Indians abroad, bringing in roughly $34 billion. He also raises the repo rate to fight inflation.

events.title: Stability returns
events.description: The rupee recovers to the low 60s per dollar, the current account deficit shrinks sharply, and the Sensex reaches a new record high near 21,500.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: In May 2013 the US Federal Reserve only hinted that it might slow its bond purchases, yet the rupee fell about 20% within three months. Why was India hit so hard?
options: India had pegged the rupee to the US dollar
India was running a record current account deficit funded by foreign capital, so any sign of tighter global money threatened that funding
The RBI had cut interest rates to zero
Indian shares were not open to foreign investors
body.explanation: A country that spends more abroad than it earns must attract foreign money every month to fill the gap. When global credit looks set to tighten, investors pull back first from the countries most dependent on that money. India's 4.8% of GDP current account deficit and high inflation made it one of the most exposed. Once gold imports were curbed and the deficit shrank, the pressure eased.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: In August 2013, India was grouped with Brazil, Indonesia, South Africa and Turkey as the ___ Five, economies seen as most vulnerable to foreign money leaving.
body.explanation: The label, coined in a Morgan Stanley research note, captured economies with large current account deficits and high inflation. Within about a year India had moved out of the group in most investors' eyes, as its deficit shrank and inflation began to fall.

children.text: A Flat Index, Two Very Different Markets

A flat Sensex hid an enormous split underneath. Businesses that did not need heavy borrowing or government approvals, and that earned in dollars or sold everyday goods with pricing power, kept growing and hit record highs. Businesses tied to the broken investment, credit and real estate cycles kept falling. The weaker rupee made the split wider, because it boosted exporters' rupee earnings while raising costs for importers and companies with foreign currency debt.

body.title: Winners and losers of the grind, 2010 to 2013

columns.label: Did well
points: FMCG companies with strong brands and pricing power, such as Hindustan Unilever and ITC
IT services exporters, helped by a weaker rupee
Private banks with cleaner loan books
Sector indices such as Nifty FMCG and Nifty IT hit record highs

columns.label: Did badly
points: Infrastructure and power developers with heavy debt
Public sector banks, carrying rising bad loans
Companies with large foreign currency borrowings

body.text: The leaders of one cycle are rarely the leaders of the next. The infrastructure, power and real estate stocks that dominated the 2003 to 2008 boom were the biggest losers of 2010 to 2013, while slow and steady consumer and IT companies that looked boring in 2007 became the market's favourites. Investors who kept buying the previous boom's winners because they looked cheap compared with their old prices were caught in Japan-style traps at the level of individual stocks.

children.text: What Worked in a Sideways Market

For a lump sum investor, a market that goes down and comes back to where it started produces a return of zero. For someone investing a fixed amount every month through a systematic investment plan, the same path produces a gain, because the falls are when the most units get bought. Here is a simplified example using a fund whose NAV falls and then recovers to its starting value.

body.title: The SIP Advantage in a Flat Market
body.prompt: Using the table above, the investor holds 491.67 units after investing ₹40,000, and the NAV is back at ₹100. What is the percentage gain on the total amount invested? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Value = 491.67 × ₹100 = ₹49,167. Gain = 49,167 ÷ 40,000 − 1 ≈ 22.9%. The NAV ended exactly where it started, so a single lump sum at ₹100 would have earned nothing. The SIP's average cost per unit was ₹40,000 ÷ 491.67 ≈ ₹81.36, because more units were bought when the price was low. The catch: this only works if the investor keeps investing through the falls, which is exactly when most people stop.

body.text: The grind years were also a period when many Indian households moved savings away from shares and into gold and real estate, both of which had risen strongly in the late 2000s amid high inflation. Gold imports became so large that they helped push the current account deficit to a record, which is why the government restricted them in 2013. Investor behaviour was following the previous cycle's winners at the macro level too.

body.title: Stop the SIP?
body.scenario: It is late August 2013. Your aunt in Kolkata has run a ₹5,000 monthly SIP in a large-cap equity fund since 2009 for her daughter's education in 2025. Her fund value is barely above what she has invested, the rupee is crashing, TV channels are calling India fragile, and gold has done far better than shares for five years. She wants to stop the SIP and buy gold coins instead.
body.prompt: Using this lesson, what would you point out to her?
body.modelAnswer: Her frustration is understandable: five years of SIPs with little to show, in a market that went sideways while inflation stayed high. But her goal is still about 12 years away, and nothing about that has changed. The reasons the market has been stuck, high inflation, stalled projects, hidden bad loans and a record current account deficit, are real, but they are cyclical problems, and 2013 was already showing signs of policy response: gold import curbs, a new RBI governor, a shrinking deficit. Stopping the SIP now would mean skipping the months when her fixed amount buys the most units, exactly the mechanism shown in this lesson's table. Switching to gold because it did well in the last five years is also chasing the previous cycle's winner, the same mistake as buying infrastructure stocks in 2010 because they led in 2007. A reasonable approach is to continue the SIP, check that the fund is a sound diversified one, and hold a modest allocation to gold if she wants diversification, decided as part of a plan rather than as a reaction to headlines. As it happened, the Sensex hit a record high within four months and rose sharply over the following year, while gold prices fell, though nobody could have known that timing in advance.

cards.definition: The widely used description of delayed government decisions on projects, mining and reforms in India around 2011 to 2013.
A large fiscal deficit and a large current account deficit at the same time, leaving a country dependent on foreign capital.
The 2013 sell-off in emerging market currencies, bonds and shares after the US Fed signalled it could slow its bond purchases.
Brazil, India, Indonesia, South Africa and Turkey, grouped in 2013 as economies most vulnerable to capital outflows.
Changing the terms of a struggling borrower's loan, such as extending repayment. Widely used in India before 2015 in ways that delayed the recognition of bad loans.
A long period in which an index moves within a range without making lasting progress. Lump sums earn little, while regular investing can still produce gains.

body.label: AMFI: Mutual Fund Industry Data
body.description: The Association of Mutual Funds in India publishes monthly data on industry assets and SIP flows. Compare SIP inflows in different market phases to see how investor behaviour tracks the cycle.

children.text: On 16 May 2014 the election results gave a single party a majority in the Lok Sabha for the first time in 30 years, and the Sensex crossed 25,000 during the day. The grind was over. Lesson 3.5 covers the decade that followed: reforms, a banking clean-up, the COVID crash and the rise of domestic SIP money as a force that changed how Indian market cycles behave.

body.text: Index levels, exchange rates, inflation and other figures in this lesson are approximate and rounded, and some data has since been revised. The SIP table is a simplified illustration, not the performance of any real fund. Company and sector references describe historical trends for education only, and nothing here is a recommendation or investment advice.

points: After a fast rebound helped by rate cuts, stimulus and a one-day 17% rally in May 2009, the Sensex stalled between roughly 15,000 and 21,000 for three years
Inflation near 10%, 13 rate hikes, stalled projects, governance shocks, hidden bad loans and a record current account deficit kept the cycle from turning up
The January 2008 investor was back to nominal break-even around December 2013, but with inflation near 9% a year had lost roughly 40% in purchasing power
The 2013 taper tantrum pushed the rupee to about 68.85 per dollar and India into the Fragile Five, until gold curbs, RBI action and a smaller deficit restored stability
A flat index hid a split market: FMCG, IT and pharma exporters hit records while infrastructure, real estate and public sector banks slumped
In a market that falls and returns to its starting level, a lump sum earns nothing, while a steady SIP can earn a solid gain, but only if it continues through the falls
